sentences.text: Efraasia was a lightly built, medium-sized sauropodomorph measuring about 6 to 7 meters in length.
This dinosaur had a slender frame with graceful hands and feet relative to its body size.
The skeleton displays two unique autapomorphies: a raised crescent-like ridge on the inner pubis shaft and a vaulted bony web connecting the braincase extensions with a central platform.
Its head featured a small, pointed, triangular skull containing four teeth in the premaxilla.
The neck was moderately elongated but remained slender in structure.
Low neural spines ran along the length of its tail.
Efraasia was once considered a tiny dinosaur, roughly 2 to 3 meters long, because the most complete fossils belonged to juveniles.
Stones found near the specimen suggest the animal swallowed gastroliths to help digest its plant food.
Master mason Albert Burrer began digging at the Weiße Steinbruch quarry near Pfaffenhofen in Württemberg in 1902.
From 1906 until the site closed in 1914, Burrer donated his finds to Professor Eberhard Fraas.
Burrer continued donating fossils found at the quarry to Professor Fraas between 1906 and 1914.
Initially, Friedrich von Huene placed Efraasia in the genus Teratosaurus in 1908 because its bones were mixed with a Rauisuchia reptile.
Eberhard Fraas discovered the initial error, retained the name for the jaw, and erected the genus Efraasia.
Friedrich von Huene described the first specimen of Efraasia in 1907–1908, originally naming it Teratosaurus minor.
Adam Yates published a comprehensive study on Efraasia fossils in 2003.
Efraasia likely exhibited facultative bipedalism, capable of walking on both two and four legs.
The animal possessed long fingers and mobile thumbs adapted for grasping food, while its wrist structure may have facilitated quadrupedal locomotion.
Like other primitive sauropodomorphs, Efraasia likely alternated between quadrupedal and bipedal locomotion.
Like many "primitive" sauropodomorphs, Efraasia may have been partially bipedal and partially quadrupedal.
Efraasia had a slender build for its size, featuring graceful hands and feet.
Efraasia possessed long fingers and mobile thumbs used for grasping food, though its wrist structure might have allowed easy quadrupedal walking.
Efraasia was a herbivore that lived approximately 210 million years ago during the Late Triassic in what is now Germany.
Efraasia minor is the only known species of the extinct genus Efraasia, a prosauropod sauropodomorph dinosaur that lived during the Late Triassic in Europe.
In 1965, Charig reclassified Efraasia as a plant-eating sauropodomorph.
Modern phylogenetic analysis places Efraasia as a basal sauropodomorph, more derived than Thecodontosaurus but less derived than Prosauropoda or Sauropoda.
Efraasia is considered a primitive sauropodomorph that is more advanced than Thecodontosaurus but less advanced than prosauropods like Plateosaurus or early sauropods like Anchisaurus.
Efraasia was found in Germany in the Lowenstein Formation in Baden-Wurttemberg and has undergone four major reclassifications.
The fossil-bearing stratum was part of the Stubensandstein member of the Lower Löwenstein Formation, dating to the Norian stage.
Some researchers debate whether Efraasia was an obligate biped, arguing that its lower arm anatomy prevented pronation and downward-facing hands.
Some researchers argue that Efraasia's lower arm structure prevented pronation, forcing it to be an obligate biped.
